reference.source: Walsh and Hoyt's Clinical Neuro-Ophthalmology / movement disorder literature
clinicalPearls: A symptomatic tremor combining rhythmic palatal movement with a synchronous pendular, often vertical, nystagmus
It develops months after a lesion in the brainstem or cerebellum affecting the triangle of Guillain and Mollaret
The delay to onset corresponds to the development of hypertrophic degeneration of the inferior olive
The pendular nystagmus causes oscillopsia and is frequently the most disabling symptom for vision
Unlike essential palatal tremor, it typically persists during sleep and is not primarily associated with an ear click
MRI characteristically shows enlargement and increased signal of the inferior olive
reference.pathophysiology: Oculopalatal tremor arises after a lesion interrupts the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway (the Guillain-Mollaret triangle), leading to transsynaptic hypertrophic degeneration of the inferior olivary nucleus. The abnormal, hypertrophied olive develops rhythmic oscillatory activity that drives synchronous rhythmic movements of the palate and the eyes, producing pendular nystagmus. The characteristic delay of months between the causative lesion and symptom onset reflects the time course of olivary hypertrophy.
additionalDifferentials: Other acquired pendular nystagmus (for example demyelinating)
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brainstem showing hypertrophic olivary degeneration
Examination of the palate and eyes for synchronous rhythmic movement
History of a preceding brainstem or cerebellar lesion
Neuro-ophthalmological assessment of the nystagmus and oscillopsia
Investigation of the underlying causative lesion if not already known
redFlags: New or progressive brainstem or cerebellar signs
An undiagnosed underlying lesion requiring evaluation
Features suggesting an alternative progressive disorder
reference.prognosis: The tremor and pendular nystagmus tend to persist and are often difficult to treat; some patients gain partial benefit from medication for the nystagmus, but the underlying olivary change is irreversible.
pitfalls: Confusing it with benign essential palatal tremor despite the nystagmus and persistence in sleep
Overlooking the typical delayed onset after a brainstem lesion
Missing hypertrophic olivary degeneration on imaging
Underestimating the visual disability from oscillopsia
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Pharmacological treatment of the disabling pendular nystagmus and oscillopsia, with gabapentin or memantine as best-supported agents and clonazepam as an alternative
Optical measures for oscillopsia, and consideration of botulinum toxin for troublesome symptomatic nystagmus or palatal movement
Identification, treatment and monitoring of the underlying brainstem or cerebellar lesion
Low-vision support and rehabilitation for persistent oscillopsia
Neurology and neuro-ophthalmology follow-up with realistic counselling, since the hypertrophic olivary change is irreversible and response is often only partial
